label: October 2026 General Conference
subtitle: 196th Semiannual General Conference · 4 sessions · coded from the official talk texts, October 11, 2026
lead: Here is one careful answer: every talk summarized, the patterns we noticed across all 37, and everything we were explicitly asked to do, starting with President Oaks.
arc: 74% of the adversity material fell on Saturday; 86% of the truth-with-love material fell on Sunday.

notes.TH01: Covenants are described as acting when the person is not: ancestors' covenants reach a descendant raised in another church, and covenants "do not 'take a day off'" (Elder Morgan, quoting President Oaks). The protection runs both ways, for the wandering child and for the faithful spouse, and three talks tie the weekly sacrament to staying on that path.
notes.TH02: The correction appears even inside a tithing talk: "This does not mean that we will be free from trials or difficulties" (Elder Giuffra). On the same Saturday, two speakers used nearly the same words for the limit of our control: Sister Runia ("something I would not be able to fix") and Elder Matthew J. Eyring's grieving friend ("I can't fix this").
notes.TH03: Grace works as connective tissue: the turn inside talks about adversity, wayward children, and teaching rather than a topic of its own. Sister Runia's sculptor and Elder Dunn's friend who quietly carried the pack make the same move: help resisted at first, then recognized.
notes.TH04: Failure is relocated from the outcome to quitting. Elder Dube's story inverts the usual sequence: the couple set a sealing date before the husband had quit smoking. Most of this theme fell in the Sunday morning session, where Elder Andersen's talk on spiritual courage and President Oaks's "We are all a work in progress" sat side by side.
notes.TH05: In every helping story the sequence is notice, then act: the frightened missionary at the airport, the janitor whose name was known, the child who unbuttoned a sleeve. President Eyring and President Chibota quoted the same line from President Kimball in the same session; the text cannot show whether that was planned.
notes.TH06: The boundary arrives inside the same talk as the love. Elder Fale warns against the lie that "because God loves us, we can be saved regardless of our pride," anticipating Sunday's truth-with-love ethic. Being known personally by God was the most widely shared idea here, appearing in 11 talks.
notes.TH07: Elder Kyungu's talk is the most practical in the conference: one list of phrases to retire and one to use. Elder Gilbert supplies the procedure (avoid overly contentious settings, find common ground, be a light, hold to truth, stay anchored in Jesus Christ) and models it with his own failure. President Uchtdorf adds the reason: "If we are not one, we are not His."
notes.TH08: Digital risk recurs across three sessions: mobile gambling (President Christofferson), "artificial information" (Elder Andersen), coarse online speech (Elder Cook), sleep and phone limits (Sister Muñoz Spannaus). Practices are the means, never the message, which is why this theme reaches 24 talks but with few passages in each.
notes.TH09: Elder Soares on fasting and President Christofferson on gambling spoke in the same Saturday morning session. President Christofferson's is the only talk built on survey data. The two tithing talks divide the promise: Elder Giuffra stresses the test of faith, Elder Villanueva the discipline of noticing blessings already received.
notes.TH10: Witness runs from the top down (apostolic witness, a family that sailed through a storm to hear an Apostle) and from the bottom up (a niece's two sentences, a Primary child's song, a 25-minute Sunday School lesson). President Oaks extends the invitation to all nations and teaches that grace is for all, on conditions the Savior has set. This was the pattern we noticed in the most talks: 25 of 37.

speaker_note: All twelve members of the Quorum of the Twelve spoke. Three of the 36 speakers were women, all general officers. The First Presidency row excludes President Oaks's short closing remarks.
scripture_highlights: Four chapters were cited in seven talks each: Mosiah 18 (the baptismal covenant), Moroni 10, Matthew 7, and Doctrine and Covenants 88.

Shared stories: the good Samaritan (President Farnes, President Chibota), the woman at the well (President Chibota, Elder Sinclair), the rich young man (President Chibota, Sister Muñoz Spannaus), Malachi's windows of heaven (Elder Giuffra, Elder Villanueva), Alma the Younger (Elder Caussé, Elder Rasband), Jairus's daughter (Elder Hathaway, Elder Kearon), and Lehi's dream (Elder Rasband, Elder Stevenson).

theory_note: Mapped after coding. Eleven of 25 thematic categories map to no construct; two are candidate contributions: covenant reach (a commitment acting on people who never made it) and God works through people (promised help delivered through third parties). Quality of theory use: applied (Painter et al., 2008).

design: What did the conference teach, how was it distributed across speakers and sessions, and what did speakers ask listeners to do?
Qualitative content analysis with thematic synthesis; descriptive claims only
Census of all 37 addresses by 36 speakers in four general sessions (44,163 words), from the official published texts
Published paragraph within an address (932 meaning units)
Two-cycle coding (Saldaña, 2013): 1,801 code applications, 124 codes, 26 categories, 10 themes
Single coder: an AI language model (Claude, Anthropic) following a written protocol
Unit file with stable IDs, range-coded assignments, codebook and log, memos, scripts
paragraphs: The official text of each address as published by the Church at churchofjesuschrist.org, retrieved October 11, 2026. Speaker names, callings, and talk titles are taken from those pages. The sustaining of officers, conducting remarks, prayers, and music are excluded, as are section headings, footnote text, and picture captions. An earlier pass of this study used machine transcripts of the broadcast; it was redone in full from the official texts, and this site reports only the redone study.

All 932 units read in full and coded in talk order, one to three codes each: Initial coding by default, In Vivo where the speaker's words carried the concept, Process coding for actions. A code exists only with a one-sentence definition and inclusion and exclusion rules. One analytic memo per talk.

Open, axial, and selective coding (Williams & Moser, 2019): codes grouped into 26 categories, then ten themes stated as claims. Constant comparison throughout. Rhetorical moves coded but held out of the themes. Theme count set by the principal investigator.

Pattern search for invitation language across all units, then a full reading of each talk's directive passages. Kept only explicit invitations and direct instructions to listeners (subgroups flagged); promises, wishes, and descriptions excluded; each anchored to a verbatim quote.

Word counts, word frequencies, Christ-reference density, leader mentions, and recurring phrases produced by deterministic scripts. Talk lengths come from the official video durations. Scripture references are counted from each talk's official footnotes and in-text citations; references to study aids (Guide to the Scriptures, Bible Dictionary, Topical Guide) are not counted.
trust: All 186 excerpts in the invitation list and example tables verified by script to appear word for word in the cited unit of the official text.
Rerunning the unit script reproduces all 932 units exactly; workbook counts are live formulas.
Codebook definitions, codebook log, and one memo per talk in the workbook.
Claims scoped to this conference; master codebook supports future comparison.
Blind double-code of one talk prepared with Cohen's kappa; threshold 0.61 (Landis & Koch, 1977). Not yet completed.
method.reflexivity: Coding was performed by an AI language model working from the written protocol; the principal investigator set the scope and is responsible for reviewing the output. An AI coder is consistent and fully documented but can repeat a blind spot across passes, so a human double-code is required before publication.
limitations: The published text can differ slightly from what was spoken from the pulpit; this study follows the published text.
Units follow the published paragraph breaks, so talks written in short paragraphs yield more units than talks written in long ones.
Ten themes exceed the usual five to seven; themes 4 and 8 are broad but thin.
Theory mappings are cross-context and partly analogical (Venkatesh, Thong & Xu, 2016).
Single coder; agreement not yet measured.

steps: All 37 addresses from the four general sessions, taken from the official texts published by the Church.
A script splits each talk into its published paragraphs: 932 meaning units with stable IDs, so every claim can point to a unit.
Every unit read in full and given one to three codes (Initial, In Vivo, Process). A code exists only with a definition plus inclusion and exclusion rules.
Each new unit is compared with units already in its code; definitions are tightened, and merges and rule changes are logged.
Codes are grouped into categories (axial), then integrated into ten themes stated as claims (selective). Rhetorical moves are coded but kept out of the themes.
Every quotation is checked by script against the official text; theory is consulted only after the themes exist; a blind double-code tests agreement.
method.saturation_note: All 26 categories had appeared by the 10th talk; after that, talks added new codes (talk-specific concepts) at a rate of 0 to 6 each but no new categories. The thematic structure was saturated well before the corpus ended (Guest, Bunce & Johnson, 2006).
method.standards: Reporting follows the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (O'Brien et al., 2014) and the relevant COREQ items (Tong, Sainsbury & Craig, 2007). Thematic synthesis follows Braun and Clarke (2006); reliability follows O'Connor and Joffe's (2020) guidance for intercoder agreement in qualitative research.

site.name: What Did They Say?
site.tagline: What did they say in the last general conference? The answer, every six months.
site.disclaimer: What Did They Say? is an independent study aid. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Quotations come from the official talk texts; read, watch, and listen to the talks themselves at churchofjesuschrist.org.
site.hero: What did they say in the last general conference?

five_min: Witness and invitation was the pattern we noticed in the most talks: 25 of 37. Christ as the one who carries and lifts was close behind, in 23.
Saturday dwelt on trials (74% of the adversity material); Sunday turned to how we treat each other (86% of the truth-with-love material).

President Oaks asked us to focus on developing faith in Christ, hold on to the first article of faith, keep our commandments and covenants, protect ourselves through the sacrament, believe the Book of Mormon's promises, act on and share these truths, and study the talks.
"Love" in its forms appears 263 times, far more than "covenant" (158) or "temple" (77).

quiz.q: Which day carried most of the talk about trials and adversity?
quiz.why: 74% of the adversity material fell on Saturday.

quiz.q: Sister Runia said the gospel isn't the ___; it's the solid rock.
quiz.why: “The gospel isn’t the umbrella; it’s the solid rock we’re standing on during the storm.”
Love and its forms: 263. Covenant(s): 158. Temple(s): 77.

quiz.q: How many of the other 35 talks mentioned President Oaks?
quiz.why: He was mentioned in 21 and quoted in 15.

quiz.q: Which speaker made the case against gambling?
quiz.why: All 30 uses of “gambling” and its forms came from President Christofferson's talk.
